Thanks Marissa — helpful summary. A few answers and clarifications from our side: 

- Traffic profile: ~120 req/min today for conversational endpoints, peak 500 req/min during batch ingest windows. Typical prompt lengths ~200 tokens, generation avg 150 tokens. Embeddings: 300 calls/min during indexing windows.
- Auth: we prefer API keys integrated with our KMS (no mTLS for now). Keys are rotated every 90 days.
- SLOs: 95th pct latency target 600ms for chat responses; 99th pct ideally < 1.5s. Error budget tight — procurement will push on SLA language.

Questions for Redwood team:
1) For 429 handling: do you recommend client-side exponential backoff + jitter and request IDs for idempotency?
2) For reranker flow: is it better to do embeddings -> candidate generation -> rerank in a single pipeline call (atomic) or separate calls so we can cache embeddings?

Happy to provide logs and sample payloads. Can we do the architecture review Thurs 26th?

Alex — nice to meet you (virtually). Prefer to keep the reply focused on architecture options and pragmatic recommendations.

1) SDK & auth
- Quickstart: use our Node/Python SDK to manage connections and retries; SDK supports API key + optional mTLS. For KMS rotations, recommend rotating keys in our console and using short-lived delegated tokens if you want zero-downtime rotation.

2) Routing / quotas
- We can route by customer/team via the API key and apply per-key quotas and rate limits. For your peaks (500 RPS during windows) we suggest a dedicated capacity pool or reserved throughput with predictable burst capacity.

3) Embeddings + reranker patterns
- Two patterns: (A) Separate pipeline: compute embeddings, store in your vector DB, generate candidate set, then call our reranker on a small candidate list. Pros: cacheable embeddings, lower rerank cost. Cons: additional network hops.
- (B) Atomic pipeline: call an orchestrator service that does embed->candidate->rerank in one server-side flow. Pros: simpler orchestration, potential for server-side cache. Cons: less cacheability and higher per-request cost.

4) Structured output & tool calling
- For triage flow, we recommend function/tool calling with strict schema validation to avoid hallucination. Our SDK supports schema-first calls and will validate outputs; we can send suggested JSON schema for your triage object.

5) Rate limits / retries / idempotency (high level)
- Client-side: exponential backoff with full jitter, capped retries (3-5 attempts depending on idempotency). Use unique request IDs (uuid v4) for non-idempotent operations and replay-safe ids for batch or async workloads.
- Server-side: 429 includes Retry-After header when queue-backed; for per-key throttles we return short Retry-After. For long-term quota exceed, return 403 + guidance.

I'll follow up with a short doc that includes recommended backoff parameters and a sample middleware snippet for request IDs.

—Ben

Priya — quick answers and included attachment (SOW-Acme-v1.pdf) in thread. TL;DR:

429 semantics
- We include Retry-After (seconds) for queue/backpressure scenarios and may omit it for token bucket immediate throttles; clients should treat missing Retry-After as "apply backoff policy and consult X-RateLimit-* headers".
- We also surface X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset headers on most endpoints to allow client-side pacing.

Idempotency
- Yes, we accept Idempotency-Key on write/batch endpoints. The server will dedupe identical requests with the same key for a configurable window (default 5 minutes). For long-running async jobs we return a 202 with Location header to poll.

Retry recommendations (recommended middleware snippet included in rate-limit-handling.md)
- For safe (idempotent) operations: up to 5 retries with exponential backoff starting at 100ms, multiplier 2, full jitter, max backoff 5s.
- For non-idempotent operations: prefer client-side request IDs + single retry guarded by server-side idempotency key.
- For 429 with Retry-After: immediately respect Retry-After + randomized jitter before next attempt.

Operational notes
- We can configure per-key quotas and will surface quota alerts to your team. If you sign up for Dedicated/Reserved capacity we can bump limits and provide SLA language.

Attaching: SOW-Acme-v1.pdf (contract draft). I also attached the recommended middleware and a quick SDK example for handling 429s and idempotency.

Let me know if you want an architecture sync Thurs 26th or Fri 27th — Marissa can schedule.
